When these US coin designs debuted.Lincoln cent: The first US circulating coin to show a real person, it marked the centennial of Lincoln's birth.
When these US coin designs debuted.Buffalo nickel: The bison on the back was said to be modeled on Black Diamond, a resident of the New York zoo, and the Native American face was a composite.
When these US coin designs debuted.Washington quarter: Issued to mark the 200th anniversary of Washington's birth, it replaced the Standing Liberty quarter.
When these US coin designs debuted.Jefferson nickel: It shows Jefferson's home Monticello, and from 1942 to 1945 wartime nickels contained silver to save nickel metal.
When these US coin designs debuted.Roosevelt dime: The coin came the year after Franklin D. Roosevelt's death, and he was linked to the March of Dimes fight against polio.
When these US coin designs debuted.Kennedy half dollar: Issued months after the assassination in 1964, it sold out quickly, and it was the last half dollar made mostly of silver.
When these US coin designs debuted.Susan B. Anthony dollar: The first US circulating coin to depict a real woman was often mistaken for a quarter because of its size and color.
When these US coin designs debuted.50 State Quarters: This program issued five new designs each year through 2008, and it made millions of Americans start collecting coins.
When these US coin designs debuted.Sacagawea dollar: It honored the Shoshone guide of Lewis and Clark, shown carrying her infant son, and has a golden color from manganese brass.
When these US coin designs debuted.Color-tinted $20 bill: The tinted bill, with peach and blue shades, was meant to deter counterfeiters and was one of a series of redesigns.

Countries by length of coastline.Monaco: Monaco's coast is only a few kilometres long, and the whole country is smaller than New York's Central Park.
Countries by length of coastline.Bosnia and Herzegovina: Bosnia has a tiny stretch of Adriatic coast around Neum, which splits Croatia in two and gives Bosnia its only sea access.
Countries by length of coastline.Belgium: Belgium's short North Sea coast is lined with resorts, and a tram line runs along it for nearly its entire length.
Countries by length of coastline.Poland: Poland's Baltic coast has long sandy beaches and the famous moving dunes of Slowinski National Park.
Countries by length of coastline.Germany: Germany has coastlines on both the North and Baltic Seas, including tidal flats that are a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
Countries by length of coastline.Spain: Spain has coasts on the Atlantic and the Mediterranean, plus islands like the Balearics and Canaries.
Countries by length of coastline.Italy: Italy is a boot-shaped peninsula and has a long coast as well as the islands of Sicily and Sardinia.
Countries by length of coastline.Mexico: Mexico borders both the Pacific and the Gulf of Mexico, with the Caribbean coast of the Yucatan too.
Countries by length of coastline.Indonesia: Indonesia is the world's biggest island nation, with over 17,000 islands, so it has huge coastlines.
Countries by length of coastline.Canada: Canada has the longest coastline of any country, thanks in large part to its Arctic islands and three oceans.

How we pay: milestones in money.Lydian coins: Merchants in western Turkey struck these from electrum, a natural gold-silver mix, and King Croesus later issued pure gold and silver coins.
How we pay: milestones in money.Chinese jiaozi paper money: The Song dynasty's jiaozi grew from merchants' deposit receipts in Sichuan, before the state took over and issued the first widely used paper money.
How we pay: milestones in money.Stockholms Banco notes: Johan Palmstruch's bank issued Europe's first banknotes, but he printed too many, the bank failed, and he was sentenced to death before being pardoned.
How we pay: milestones in money.AmEx traveler's cheque: The American Express cheque was made so travellers could carry safe money abroad after a company executive struggled to cash funds in Europe.
How we pay: milestones in money.Diners Club card: The story goes that founder Frank McNamara forgot his wallet at a New York restaurant, which sparked the first general charge card.
How we pay: milestones in money.Discover card: Sears launched it with an unusual perk, cash back on purchases, which no major card had offered before.
How we pay: milestones in money.PayPal founded: Founded by Peter Thiel and Max Levchin as Confinity, it merged with Elon Musk's X.com, and eBay bought it in 2002.
How we pay: milestones in money.Euro notes and coins: Notes and coins reached wallets on 1 January 2002 in twelve countries, though the currency had existed in digital form since 1999.
How we pay: milestones in money.M-Pesa: Launched by Safaricom in Kenya, 'M' stands for mobile and 'pesa' is Swahili for money. It lets people send cash without a bank account.
How we pay: milestones in money.Apple Pay: Launched with the iPhone 6, it replaces your real card number with a one-time token, so shops never see the actual number.

Camera milestones, oldest to newest.Daguerreotype: Made by Louis Daguerre, each was a one-of-a-kind image on a silvered copper plate, with no negative to make copies.
Camera milestones, oldest to newest.First colour photograph: Physicist James Clerk Maxwell had it taken of a tartan ribbon by combining three black-and-white plates with coloured filters.
Camera milestones, oldest to newest.Kodak box camera: George Eastman's slogan was 'You press the button, we do the rest': it came preloaded with film for 100 exposures.
Camera milestones, oldest to newest.Leica 35mm camera: Oskar Barnack built a prototype around 1913. It used cine film, putting a small camera in every photographer's pocket.
Camera milestones, oldest to newest.Kodachrome film: Paul Simon sang about it in 1973. Kodak stopped making it in 2009 and the last lab to process it closed in 2010.
Camera milestones, oldest to newest.Polaroid instant camera: Edwin Land launched it after his three-year-old daughter asked why she couldn't see a photo he'd just taken.
Camera milestones, oldest to newest.Kodak Instamatic: Its drop-in film cartridge needed no threading and sold in the tens of millions, putting snapshots into everyone's hands.
Camera milestones, oldest to newest.Digital camera prototype: Kodak engineer Steven Sasson built it, a toaster-sized device that took 23 seconds to record a 0.01-megapixel image.
Camera milestones, oldest to newest.Disposable camera: Fuji's QuickSnap launched in 1986 and Kodak followed. These cheap cameras are popular again for their film look.
Camera milestones, oldest to newest.GoPro: Nick Woodman created it for surfers with a wrist strap, and the first model used 35mm film.

Crops and fruits: when they came along.Wheat farming begins: Early farmers in the Fertile Crescent began growing it, and today it is cultivated on more land than any other crop.
Crops and fruits: when they came along.Cacao first used: Evidence from the Ecuadorian Amazon suggests people used it long before the Maya; chocolate began as a bitter drink.
Crops and fruits: when they came along.Coffee farmed in Yemen: Sufi monks in Yemen used it to stay awake during night prayers, and the port of Mocha lent its name to a style of coffee.
Crops and fruits: when they came along.Garden strawberry bred: It came from crossing a Virginian and a Chilean strawberry in French gardens, a happy accident of the 1700s.
Crops and fruits: when they came along.Granny Smith apple: Australian grower Maria Ann Smith found the seedling in her garden in 1868, and her name is still on the apple.
Crops and fruits: when they came along.Kiwifruit seeds reach NZ: First called the Chinese gooseberry, it was renamed for the kiwi bird in the 1950s to help it sell abroad.
Crops and fruits: when they came along.Gala apple: New Zealand's J. H. Kidd bred it in the 1930s by crossing Kidd's Orange Red with Golden Delicious.
Crops and fruits: when they came along.Pluot: Floyd Zaiger's plum-apricot hybrid is mostly plum, and the name pluot is a trademarked blend of the two fruits.
Crops and fruits: when they came along.Honeycrisp released: Developed at the University of Minnesota, its large cells are what give it an explosive crunch.
Crops and fruits: when they came along.Cosmic Crisp released: Washington State University's apple took about twenty years to develop, a cross between Enterprise and Honeycrisp.

Driving nonstop at 100 km/h to....Top of Everest (straight up): Everest is about 8.8 km high, so a car would reach the top in about 5 minutes if it could drive straight up, as the title suggests.
Driving nonstop at 100 km/h to....Once around the equator: Earth's equator is about 40,075 km around, and driving it at 100 km/h would take about 17 days, with no stops.
Driving nonstop at 100 km/h to....The Moon: The Moon is about 384,000 km away, and a car would need around five months to reach it.
Driving nonstop at 100 km/h to....Venus (at closest): Venus is about 40 million km away at its closest, and that's about 43 years of nonstop driving.
Driving nonstop at 100 km/h to....Mars (at closest): Mars sits about 55 million km away at its nearest, and Mars rovers take around seven months to get there instead.
Driving nonstop at 100 km/h to....The Sun: The Sun is about 150 million km away, and light takes just over eight minutes to make that trip.
Driving nonstop at 100 km/h to....Jupiter (at closest): Jupiter is roughly 590 million km at its closest, and its Great Red Spot is a storm bigger than Earth.
Driving nonstop at 100 km/h to....Neptune (at closest): Neptune is so far away that it takes light over four hours to arrive, and it was discovered by mathematical prediction.
Driving nonstop at 100 km/h to....Proxima Centauri: Proxima Centauri is the nearest star beyond the Sun, at about 4.2 light-years away, and it has an Earth-sized planet.
Driving nonstop at 100 km/h to....Andromeda Galaxy: The Andromeda Galaxy is about 2.5 million light-years away, and it is on a collision course with our Milky Way.

Traditional wedding anniversary gifts.Paper: The first anniversary gift suggests a blank page, beginning a new story together.
Traditional wedding anniversary gifts.Cotton: The second-year gift of cotton is linked to the idea of a growing, comfortable partnership.
Traditional wedding anniversary gifts.Leather: The third-year gift of leather stands for durability and strength.
Traditional wedding anniversary gifts.Wood: Wood stands for roots; the fifth anniversary is when a couple's marriage is thought to have strong roots.
Traditional wedding anniversary gifts.Tin: A tin gift is traditional because the metal is flexible yet durable, and modern lists often replace it with aluminum.
Traditional wedding anniversary gifts.Crystal: The 15th anniversary gift of crystal stands for clarity and transparency in the relationship.
Traditional wedding anniversary gifts.China: Fine china is a gift that is both beautiful and fragile, and is the traditional 20th anniversary present.
Traditional wedding anniversary gifts.Silver: Silver for the 25th gives it the nickname silver jubilee.
Traditional wedding anniversary gifts.Ruby: Ruby symbolizes passion that lasts, as the deep red stone suggests love that is still burning at 40 years.
Traditional wedding anniversary gifts.Gold: Gold for the 50th anniversary is known as the golden jubilee.

Number words from around the world, by v.dozen: Twelve divides evenly by 2, 3, 4 and 6, handy for splitting goods, and a baker's dozen is 13.
Number words from around the world, by v.score: Lincoln's Four score and seven years ago means 87 years; the word probably comes from notches counted on a tally stick.
Number words from around the world, by v.gross: A dozen dozen, it was long a merchant's unit for bulk items such as pencils or buttons.
Number words from around the world, by v.great gross: This is twelve gross, or a dozen cubed, and it is rarely used outside old-fashioned wholesale trade.
Number words from around the world, by v.myriad: From a Greek word for 10,000, it now just means countless, though in Chinese the character wan still means exactly 10,000.
Number words from around the world, by v.lakh: Indian numbering groups digits by lakhs and crores, so 100,000 is written 1,00,000 in India.
Number words from around the world, by v.million: A million seconds is about 11.5 days, while a billion seconds is more than 31 years.
Number words from around the world, by v.crore: Budgets and film box-office figures in India are routinely quoted in crores.
Number words from around the world, by v.billion (short scale): Britain officially switched in 1974 from the long scale, where a billion meant a million million, to the American short scale.
Number words from around the world, by v.googol: It was reportedly coined by the nine-year-old nephew of mathematician Edward Kasner, and it inspired the name Google.

How many times married?.Ross Geller: Ross marries Carol, Emily and Rachel on Friends, and his three weddings, including a drunken Vegas one, fuel the show's running 'divorced' gag.
How many times married?.Charlie Chaplin: The silent-film star wed four times, and the last wife, Oona O'Neill, stayed with him until his death in 1977, bearing eight children.
How many times married?.Henry VIII: A rhyme sums up his six wives as 'divorced, beheaded, died, divorced, beheaded, survived', and he broke with Rome to wed the second.
How many times married?.Jerry Lee Lewis: The rock and roll pianist's marriage to his 13-year-old cousin Myra caused a scandal that wrecked his 1958 British tour.
How many times married?.Elizabeth Taylor: The actress wed eight times, to seven men, as she married Richard Burton twice, the second time in Botswana in 1975.
How many times married?.Zsa Zsa Gabor: One of the Hungarian-born Gabor sisters, she wed nine times, and her husbands included hotel magnate Conrad Hilton and actor George Sanders.
How many times married?.Linda Wolfe: Guinness recognized her as the most married woman, with 23 marriages, and her final husband was herself record-holder Glynn Wolfe.
How many times married?.Glynn Wolfe: Known as Scotty, this preacher from Oklahoma was recorded by Guinness as the most married man in history, with 29 weddings by the end.
How many times married?.Brigham Young: The Mormon leader who led pioneers to Utah in 1847 is generally said to have had over 50 wives, a practice the church later abandoned.
How many times married?.King Solomon: Per the Bible, this king of Israel had 700 wives and 300 concubines, which is tough to square with his reputation for wisdom.

How deep you'd have to go to reach it.Recreational scuba limit: Recreational scuba is capped at 40 meters because deeper, nitrogen narcosis can cloud judgment, a bit like drinking.
How deep you'd have to go to reach it.End of the sunlight zone: The sunlight zone ends at around 200 meters, below which only a faint twilight remains, and photosynthesis ends.
How deep you'd have to go to reach it.Lake Superior's deepest point: Lake Superior is the biggest freshwater lake by area, and its deep cold water is why shipwrecks there are so well preserved.
How deep you'd have to go to reach it.Lake Baikal's deepest point: Lake Baikal in Siberia is the deepest lake in the world, and holds about a fifth of the world's unfrozen fresh water.
How deep you'd have to go to reach it.Black Sea's deepest point: The Black Sea's deep waters have almost no oxygen, which means shipwrecks there have been preserved for centuries.
How deep you'd have to go to reach it.Wreck of the Titanic: The Titanic lies in two main pieces on the seafloor, and it is slowly being eaten away by iron-eating bacteria.
How deep you'd have to go to reach it.Mediterranean's Calypso Deep: The Calypso Deep, in the Ionian Sea, is the deepest point in the Mediterranean, and was named after the research vessel Calypso.
How deep you'd have to go to reach it.Java (Sunda) Trench: The Java Trench is the deepest point of the Indian Ocean, and it is caused by a tectonic plate sliding beneath another.
How deep you'd have to go to reach it.Puerto Rico Trench: The Puerto Rico Trench is the deepest in the Atlantic Ocean, and the region is prone to earthquakes and tsunamis.
How deep you'd have to go to reach it.Challenger Deep: The Challenger Deep, at the bottom of the Mariana Trench, has been reached by only a handful of people, including filmmaker James Cameron in 2012.

Nobel Prize in Medicine: when these were.Malaria spread by mosquitoes: Ronald Ross showed the link while working in India, and won in 1902 for tracing malaria parasites in mosquitoes.
Nobel Prize in Medicine: when these were.Tuberculosis bacterium: Robert Koch identified the bacterium in 1882, and in 1905 won the prize for his work on tuberculosis.
Nobel Prize in Medicine: when these were.Insulin: Frederick Banting and John Macleod shared it, and Banting sold the patent for $1 to the University of Toronto.
Nobel Prize in Medicine: when these were.Penicillin: Alexander Fleming noticed in 1928 that a mold killed bacteria on a dish, and Florey and Chain turned it into a drug.
Nobel Prize in Medicine: when these were.Structure of DNA: Rosalind Franklin's X-ray images were key to the discovery, but she died in 1958, before the prize went to Watson, Crick and Wilkins.
Nobel Prize in Medicine: when these were.Prions: Stanley Prusiner won for prions, misfolded proteins that cause diseases such as mad cow disease.
Nobel Prize in Medicine: when these were.Stomach-ulcer bacterium: To prove it, Barry Marshall drank a culture of the bacteria and developed gastritis, and shared the prize with Robin Warren.
Nobel Prize in Medicine: when these were.IVF: Robert Edwards won for it, three decades after the first IVF baby, Louise Brown, was born in 1978.
Nobel Prize in Medicine: when these were.Artemisinin for malaria: Tu Youyou found the drug by studying ancient Chinese herbal texts on sweet wormwood.
Nobel Prize in Medicine: when these were.mRNA vaccines: Katalin Karikó and Drew Weissman won for the technology that made COVID-19 vaccines possible within a year.

Fictional lands, by when readers first v.Lilliput: Jonathan Swift's tiny kingdom of Gulliver's Travels is home to people about six inches tall, and a satire of English politics.
Fictional lands, by when readers first v.Wonderland: Lewis Carroll first told the story to Alice Liddell and her sisters on a boat trip along the Thames in Oxford.
Fictional lands, by when readers first v.Oz: In L. Frank Baum's book Dorothy's magic slippers were silver; the movie changed them to ruby red to show off Technicolor.
Fictional lands, by when readers first v.Neverland: J. M. Barrie's play Peter Pan premiered in 1904, and he left the rights to Great Ormond Street Hospital.
Fictional lands, by when readers first v.The Shire: Tolkien introduced it in The Hobbit, with its rolling, quiet countryside modelled on the English Midlands where he grew up.
Fictional lands, by when readers first v.Narnia: C. S. Lewis reportedly took the name from Narni, an Italian town he found in an atlas.
Fictional lands, by when readers first v.Discworld: Terry Pratchett's flat world rests on the backs of four elephants who stand on a giant turtle called Great A'Tuin.
Fictional lands, by when readers first v.Westeros: George R. R. Martin took inspiration partly from England's Wars of the Roses for this realm.
Fictional lands, by when readers first v.Hogwarts: In 1997, J. K. Rowling's school of magic took its name from a hogwort plant she'd seen at Kew Gardens.
Fictional lands, by when readers first v.Panem: The name comes from the Latin 'panem et circenses', or bread and circuses, the Romans' way of keeping a crowd distracted.

When our lineage split from theirs.Zebrafish: Zebrafish embryos are transparent, so scientists watch organs form live, and the adults can even regrow damaged heart tissue.
When our lineage split from theirs.Chicken: Birds are living dinosaurs, and the chicken's genome, published in 2004, was the first of a bird to be sequenced.
When our lineage split from theirs.House mouse: Mice share most of our genes, and the lab mouse is the workhorse of medical research, so this branch is well studied.
When our lineage split from theirs.Mouse lemur: Native to Madagascar, these tiny nocturnal primates are among the smallest in the world, and some weigh little more than a small hamster.
When our lineage split from theirs.Marmoset: Common marmosets take turns when calling, like a conversation, and usually give birth to twins that the whole family helps carry.
When our lineage split from theirs.Rhesus macaque: The Rh blood group, as in Rh-positive, is named after the rhesus monkey, in which it was first found.
When our lineage split from theirs.Gibbon: These small apes swing arm over arm through the trees and sing duets with their mates that carry for kilometres.
When our lineage split from theirs.Orangutan: The name is Malay for 'person of the forest', and these red apes spend most of their lives high in trees.
When our lineage split from theirs.Gorilla: Gorillas build a fresh nest every night out of leaves and branches, and share about 98 percent of our DNA.
When our lineage split from theirs.Chimpanzee: With bonobos, chimps are our closest living relatives, and they strip twigs to fish termites out of their mounds.

Brightness in Earth's sky, at their best.The Sun: It is about 400,000 times brighter than the full Moon.
Brightness in Earth's sky, at their best.Full Moon: Its brightness changes with its phase, and a full Moon is far brighter than a half Moon.
Brightness in Earth's sky, at their best.International Space Station: Its solar panels reflect sunlight so brightly that it can outshine Venus as it crosses the sky in minutes.
Brightness in Earth's sky, at their best.Venus: The brightest planet, thanks to thick clouds that reflect sunlight, it is sometimes visible in daytime.
Brightness in Earth's sky, at their best.Jupiter: Binoculars reveal its four biggest moons, which Galileo spotted in 1610.
Brightness in Earth's sky, at their best.Sirius: The brightest star in the night sky, only about 8.6 light years away; also called the Dog Star.
Brightness in Earth's sky, at their best.Polaris: The North Star is not especially bright, but it sits almost exactly above Earth's north pole and barely moves.
Brightness in Earth's sky, at their best.Uranus: It was the first planet found with a telescope; William Herschel first thought it was a comet in 1781.
Brightness in Earth's sky, at their best.Dark-sky naked-eye limit: This limit comes from the ancient magnitude scale, which ranked the brightest stars as 1 and the faintest visible as 6.
Brightness in Earth's sky, at their best.Pluto: Clyde Tombaugh discovered it in 1930; it was reclassified as a dwarf planet in 2006, and you need a telescope to see it.

Winter Olympics host towns.Chamonix: The 1924 Games here were originally billed as 'International Winter Sports Week' and only later declared the first Winter Olympics, beneath Mont Blanc.
Winter Olympics host towns.Garmisch-Partenkirchen: The 1936 Games in this Bavarian twin town were held under Nazi Germany, and were the first to include alpine skiing.
Winter Olympics host towns.Oslo: In 1952 the Games' flame was lit in the fireplace of the home of skiing pioneer Sondre Norheim, in Morgedal, rather than in Greece.
Winter Olympics host towns.Squaw Valley: In 1960 this California resort held the first Games where a computer, from IBM, was used to tabulate results. The resort has since dropped the name.
Winter Olympics host towns.Grenoble: The 1968 Games came with the first Olympic mascot, a skier named Schuss, and were the first broadcast in colour.
Winter Olympics host towns.Sapporo: In 1972 this became the first Winter Games in Asia, held in Japan's snowiest big city, which also hosts a famous annual snow festival.
Winter Olympics host towns.Sarajevo: The 1984 Games were a celebrated success, but the same city was besieged less than a decade later, and some venues were ruined.
Winter Olympics host towns.Albertville: The 1992 Games were spread across Savoie valleys, and were the last Winter Games held in the same year as the Summer Games.
Winter Olympics host towns.Lillehammer: These 1994 Games began a new two-year offset from the Summer Olympics, and Norway's welcome made them widely loved.
Winter Olympics host towns.Salt Lake City: The 2002 Games here are remembered for the Winter Olympics' first major judging scandal in figure skating, and for strong post-9/11 emotion.

Pioneers of medicine and biology, by bir.Hippocrates: Often called the father of medicine, he is linked to the Hippocratic Oath, though scholars doubt he wrote it. He taught that disease has natural, not divine, causes.
Pioneers of medicine and biology, by bir.Aristotle: He dissected animals and classed more than 500 species, and he tutored Alexander the Great, though he was wrong that the heart is the seat of thought.
Pioneers of medicine and biology, by bir.Galen: A Greek doctor to Roman gladiators and emperors, he shaped medicine for about 1,400 years, even though many of his anatomy claims came from animals.
Pioneers of medicine and biology, by bir.Andreas Vesalius: His 1543 book De humani corporis fabrica corrected Galen using human dissections, and its illustrations helped found modern anatomy.
Pioneers of medicine and biology, by bir.Carl Linnaeus: The Swedish botanist invented the two-part naming of species, like Homo sapiens, that scientists still use today.
Pioneers of medicine and biology, by bir.Edward Jenner: He pioneered vaccination, using cowpox, from the Latin vacca, 'cow', to protect people from smallpox, a disease that has since been eradicated.
Pioneers of medicine and biology, by bir.Gregor Mendel: This Augustinian friar discovered the basic laws of heredity by crossing thousands of pea plants, though his work was ignored until after his death.
Pioneers of medicine and biology, by bir.Robert Koch: A German physician, he identified the bacteria behind tuberculosis, cholera and anthrax, and his four postulates set rules for linking germs to disease.
Pioneers of medicine and biology, by bir.Alexander Fleming: He noticed that a mould had killed bacteria in a forgotten dish in 1928, and penicillin that came from it has saved countless lives.
Pioneers of medicine and biology, by bir.James Watson: At 25 he co-discovered the double-helix structure of DNA with Francis Crick, and he shared a Nobel Prize for it in 1962.

Counting words by quantity.Pair: The word comes from Latin par, 'equal', and in a pair the two things match, such as socks, shoes or a pair of scissors.
Counting words by quantity.Trio: Trio is borrowed from Italian, and in music it names a piece for three players, and also the contrasting middle section of a minuet.
Counting words by quantity.Dozen: The word comes from Old French dozaine, and the number 12 was popular as it divides neatly by 2, 3, 4 and 6.
Counting words by quantity.Baker's dozen: Bakers once added an extra loaf to avoid being fined for selling underweight bread in medieval England, and so the number became lucky or unlucky.
Counting words by quantity.Score: Abraham Lincoln's 'Four score and seven years ago' means 87, and it came from the Old Norse word skor, meaning notch.
Counting words by quantity.Century: The word 'century' comes from Latin centum, and in ancient Rome it could be a unit of soldiers; in cricket it means 100 runs.
Counting words by quantity.Gross: A gross is a dozen dozen, and it was used for ordering goods like buttons or pencils in bulk.
Counting words by quantity.Ream: A ream was historically 480 sheets, with 500 being the modern standard, and it comes from Arabic rizma, a bundle.
Counting words by quantity.Grand: As slang, it dates to the early 1900s and it also is a nickname for 1,000-dollar bills; also, in British slang a pound is a 'quid'.
Counting words by quantity.Myriad: This is from Greek myrias, and in English it also means a countless number of things, as in 'a myriad of stars'.

Aesop's fable animals by real weight.Ant: Ants can carry loads many times their own weight, and leafcutter ants haul leaf pieces larger than themselves, fitting the fable's hero.
Aesop's fable animals by real weight.Grasshopper: A grasshopper can leap about twenty times its body length, using springy leg tissue that stores energy like a catapult.
Aesop's fable animals by real weight.Frog: Frogs breathe partly through their skin, which is why they must stay moist. The fable's frog bursts trying to match an ox.
Aesop's fable animals by real weight.Crow: Crows can bend wire into hooks in the lab, which makes Aesop's pebble-dropping crow less fanciful than it sounds.
Aesop's fable animals by real weight.Hare: A hare can sprint at over 60 km/h, so the tortoise's win in the fable depended entirely on the hare napping.
Aesop's fable animals by real weight.Fox: Studies suggest red foxes use Earth's magnetic field to aim their pounce on prey hidden under grass or snow.
Aesop's fable animals by real weight.Wolf: Wolf packs are usually families, a breeding pair and their offspring, not the scheming gangs of fable.
Aesop's fable animals by real weight.Lion: Lions are the only truly social big cats, living in prides, and they sleep up to 20 hours a day.
Aesop's fable animals by real weight.Horse: Horses can sleep standing up, locking their legs with a system of tendons called the stay apparatus.
Aesop's fable animals by real weight.Ox: An ox is a trained adult male bovine, usually castrated, and yoked pairs pulled plows and carts for thousands of years.

Scratch test: what's harder than what?.Pencil graphite: The pencil's lead contains no lead at all. Graphite is carbon, the same element as diamond, with layers that slide off as you write.
Scratch test: what's harder than what?.Fingernail: Geologists keep this handy test in mind: a nail scratches gypsum, which is rated 2, but is itself scratched by calcite.
Scratch test: what's harder than what?.Copper coin: Fieldworkers have long used a coin as a quick test tool, since copper falls between calcite and fluorite on the scale.
Scratch test: what's harder than what?.Iron nail: Steel hardness varies by alloy, so nails give only a rough reading, but a nail still scratches calcite and many soft minerals.
Scratch test: what's harder than what?.Window glass: Quartz scratches ordinary glass easily, which is how a rock hound can tell a clear quartz crystal from a piece of glass.
Scratch test: what's harder than what?.Steel file: Hardened steel will scratch most common minerals but fails against quartz, so a file is a handy way to spot the hard ones.
Scratch test: what's harder than what?.Amethyst: Amethyst is purple quartz, and its colour comes from iron impurities plus natural irradiation in the rock where it grew.
Scratch test: what's harder than what?.Emerald: Emerald is hard but brittle, since tiny internal fractures, nicknamed the garden, run through almost every natural stone.
Scratch test: what's harder than what?.Sapphire: Sapphire is the mineral corundum; a red one is called a ruby, so the two gems are chemically the same stuff.
Scratch test: what's harder than what?.Diamond: Diamond tops the scale, yet a hard hit can still split it along its cleavage planes, because hardness is not toughness.

Inventions older than you'd think.Coin vending machine (Hero): Hero of Alexandria's machine released a little holy water when a coin dropped onto a pan.
Inventions older than you'd think.Flush toilet (Harington): Sir John Harington, Queen Elizabeth I's godson, built it and called it the Ajax, but the idea was not widely taken up for centuries.
Inventions older than you'd think.Submarine (Drebbel): Cornelis Drebbel, a Dutchman, reportedly rowed a leather-covered submarine down the Thames in London.
Inventions older than you'd think.Pascal's calculator: Blaise Pascal built the Pascaline when he was about nineteen to help his tax-collector father add up sums.
Inventions older than you'd think.Fax machine (Bain): Alexander Bain patented it in 1843, decades before the telephone existed.
Inventions older than you'd think.Rubber band: It was patented in London by Stephen Perry, and it was originally made to hold papers and envelopes together.
Inventions older than you'd think.Contact lens: Adolf Fick made the first glass versions in Switzerland, and he was working on helping people with poor eyesight.
Inventions older than you'd think.Polygraph lie detector: John Larson, a police officer and physiologist in Berkeley, built it, though most courts do not accept the results.
Inventions older than you'd think.Bubble gum: Walter Diemer made it at Fleer, and it was pink because that was the dye he had on hand.
Inventions older than you'd think.Electric toothbrush: A Swiss doctor, Philippe-Guy Woog, made it for patients with limited dexterity.

African countries by area.The Gambia: The Gambia is a thin strip along the Gambia River, almost wholly surrounded by Senegal, and is the smallest country on mainland Africa.
African countries by area.Rwanda: Called the land of a thousand hills, Rwanda is among Africa's most densely populated countries and shelters endangered mountain gorillas.
African countries by area.Senegal: Dakar, Senegal's capital, is the westernmost city on mainland Africa, and nearby Lake Retba turns pink thanks to salt-loving algae.
African countries by area.Ghana: In 1957 Ghana became the first sub-Saharan African country to win independence from colonial rule, led by Kwame Nkrumah.
African countries by area.Zimbabwe: Zimbabwe means house of stone, after the medieval ruins of Great Zimbabwe; it also shares the thundering Victoria Falls with Zambia.
African countries by area.Kenya: Mount Kenya, Africa's second-highest peak, gave the country its name, and the Maasai Mara hosts one of the planet's great wildebeest migrations.
African countries by area.Nigeria: Nigeria is Africa's most populous country, with over 200 million people and more than 500 languages spoken within its borders.
African countries by area.Egypt: Most of Egypt is desert, so nearly all its people crowd along the Nile and its delta, a small fraction of the country's land.
African countries by area.Libya: Libya is mostly Sahara, yet it holds some of Africa's largest oil reserves and the superb Roman ruins of Leptis Magna on its coast.
African countries by area.Algeria: Algeria became Africa's largest country in 2011, when South Sudan split from Sudan; most of its area is Sahara desert.

Klingon numbers, by the value they name.wa': Linguist Marc Okrand created Klingon for Star Trek III in 1984, building on a few words made up earlier; wa' means one.
Klingon numbers, by the value they name.cha': Klingon grammar puts the object first and the subject last, a rare order among real languages.
Klingon numbers, by the value they name.wej: Okrand published The Klingon Dictionary in 1985, which made the language usable beyond the movies.
Klingon numbers, by the value they name.loS: In Klingon spelling a capital S is a distinct sound, close to sh, and not the same as a lowercase s.
Klingon numbers, by the value they name.vagh: In Klingon, gh is a throaty gargle-like sound, a voiced fricative, which fits with the language's harsh feel.
Klingon numbers, by the value they name.jav: Fans translated Hamlet into Klingon, published in 2000 as The Klingon Hamlet, with taH pagh taHbe for to be or not to be.
Klingon numbers, by the value they name.Soch: Klingon has its own script, pIqaD, though almost all fans write the language in Roman letters.
Klingon numbers, by the value they name.chorgh: Klingon numbers are decimal, so ten is maH, and larger numbers stack parts together, as in wa'maH for ten.
Klingon numbers, by the value they name.Hut: Duolingo has offered a Klingon course, and there is a Klingon Language Institute with its own journal.
Klingon numbers, by the value they name.wa'maH: Klingon numbers are decimal: maH is ten, and wa'maH is literally one ten, with larger numbers stacked, as wa'maH wa' for eleven.

World health days through the calendar y.World Cancer Day: Led by the Union for International Cancer Control, this day is marked every 4 February.
World health days through the calendar y.World Health Day: This date marks the WHO's founding in 1948, and each year's event takes a different theme.
World health days through the calendar y.World Malaria Day: Malaria spreads through female Anopheles mosquitoes, and in 2021 the WHO recommended its first malaria vaccine.
World health days through the calendar y.World No Tobacco Day: Held since 1987, it highlights tobacco's toll of more than eight million deaths a year.
World health days through the calendar y.World Blood Donor Day: The date is Karl Landsteiner's birthday; he discovered the ABO blood groups in 1901.
World health days through the calendar y.World Hepatitis Day: The date is the birthday of Baruch Blumberg, who discovered hepatitis B and won a Nobel Prize in 1976.
World health days through the calendar y.World Heart Day: Founded by the World Heart Federation, it highlights that cardiovascular disease is the world's leading cause of death.
World health days through the calendar y.World Mental Health Day: Established in 1992 by the World Federation for Mental Health, it aims to reduce stigma around mental illness.
World health days through the calendar y.World Diabetes Day: The date is Frederick Banting's birthday; he co-discovered insulin in 1921.
World health days through the calendar y.World AIDS Day: Observed since 1988, it was the first ever global health day.

Old printers' names for type sizes.Diamond: The tiniest size, at 4.5 points, was used for very small text, and its name suggests a jewel more than a line of print.
Old printers' names for type sizes.Agate: Used for classified ads and sports scores, where lines had to be packed tight, and the name later gave a measure for newspaper advertising.
Old printers' names for type sizes.Nonpareil: The name is French for 'without equal'. Tiny colored sprinkles on cakes and sweets are also called nonpareils.
Old printers' names for type sizes.Minion: Adobe's Minion typeface was named after this old size, as a nod to the tradition of naming type after the point size.
Old printers' names for type sizes.Brevier: Named for the breviary, the book of daily prayers that was often printed in small type to keep it light to carry.
Old printers' names for type sizes.Bourgeois: A 9-point size. Old type names like this came from the books first printed in them or from the French founders who cast them.
Old printers' names for type sizes.Long Primer: Named for the prayer books and children's primers it was used for, and it was a common size for setting book text.
Old printers' names for type sizes.Pica: A pica is 12 points, or one sixth of an inch, and also the size of typewriter print with 10 characters per inch.
Old printers' names for type sizes.English: Its name is plain, but it dates from when each size had its own name and no number, before points were standardized.
Old printers' names for type sizes.Great Primer: Often used for headlines and large print, it is the biggest in this old series and three times the size of a nonpareil.

Booker Prize winners, by year won.Midnight's Children: Salman Rushdie's story of children born at India's independence, gifted with telepathic powers, twice won a special 'Best of the Booker'.
Booker Prize winners, by year won.Schindler's Ark: Thomas Keneally's novel on Oskar Schindler's rescue of Jews was retitled Schindler's List in America, and Spielberg filmed it.
Booker Prize winners, by year won.The Remains of the Day: Kazuo Ishiguro's butler narrator reflects on a lifetime of service; the 1993 film starred Anthony Hopkins.
Booker Prize winners, by year won.Possession: A.S. Byatt's novel has two modern scholars uncover a Victorian poets' love affair, with poems she invented herself.
Booker Prize winners, by year won.The God of Small Things: Arundhati Roy's first novel, set in Kerala, made her famous, and she didn't publish another novel for two decades.
Booker Prize winners, by year won.Life of Pi: Yann Martel's tale of a boy and a Bengal tiger on a lifeboat became an Ang Lee film in 2012.
Booker Prize winners, by year won.Wolf Hall: Hilary Mantel's tale of Thomas Cromwell began a trilogy, and she won the Booker twice, with this and its sequel.
Booker Prize winners, by year won.The Luminaries: Eleanor Catton became the youngest ever winner at 28, with a huge novel structured around astrological charts.
Booker Prize winners, by year won.Lincoln in the Bardo: George Saunders' first novel imagines a chorus of ghosts around the grave of Lincoln's young son Willie.
Booker Prize winners, by year won.Shuggie Bain: Douglas Stuart's debut, drawn from his Glasgow childhood with an alcoholic mother, was rejected by many publishers first.

When these pizza chains opened.Shakey's: The Sacramento founder paired pizza with beer and live banjo and piano music, and he turned parlors into a franchise.
When these pizza chains opened.Sbarro: It started as a Brooklyn Italian grocery, and later became a staple of shopping mall food courts.
When these pizza chains opened.Pizza Hut: Two brothers who were college students in Wichita, Kansas, borrowed about $600 to open it, and its name came from the building's hut-like shape.
When these pizza chains opened.Little Caesars: Michael Ilitch started it in a Michigan suburb, and he also owned the Detroit Red Wings hockey team.
When these pizza chains opened.Domino's: The chain began as a single store in Ypsilanti, Michigan, and later it built its brand on a promise of delivery in thirty minutes.
When these pizza chains opened.Godfather's Pizza: The Omaha-based chain was once led by presidential candidate Herman Cain, and it's known for its buffet.
When these pizza chains opened.Chuck E. Cheese: Founded by an Atari co-founder, Nolan Bushnell, this restaurant with animatronic animals added arcade games to dinner.
When these pizza chains opened.Papa John's: John Schnatter began by selling pizzas out of a converted broom closet at his father's tavern in Indiana.
When these pizza chains opened.MOD Pizza: This Seattle chain took its name from "Made on Demand", and let customers choose their toppings as in a sandwich shop.
When these pizza chains opened.Blaze Pizza: Founded in Pasadena, California, it lets diners build personal pizzas fired in minutes, and basketball star LeBron James invested in it.

Farm animals by weight.Japanese quail: The tiny quail lays speckled eggs and starts laying at around six weeks old, and its eggs are a popular snack in Asia.
Farm animals by weight.Chicken: Chickens are descended from the red junglefowl of Southeast Asia, and there are more of them on Earth than any other bird.
Farm animals by weight.Domestic goose: Geese are fiercely territorial and loud, which is why some people use them as alarm animals to guard property.
Farm animals by weight.Turkey (tom): A tom turkey can weigh more than most farm geese, and wild turkeys, unlike farm ones, can fly short distances.
Farm animals by weight.Pygmy goat: Pygmy goats are small, friendly and agile, and were originally bred in West Africa for meat and milk.
Farm animals by weight.Sheep: Sheep were among the first animals domesticated, around 10,000 years ago, and their wool has been woven since ancient times.
Farm animals by weight.Llama: Llamas are used as pack animals in the Andes and sometimes as guard animals, protecting sheep from coyotes.
Farm animals by weight.Domestic pig: Pigs are among the smartest farm animals, and studies show they can learn to play simple video games.
Farm animals by weight.Holstein cow: A Holstein cow can give over 25 liters of milk a day, which is why they are the world's top dairy breed.
Farm animals by weight.Shire horse: Shires are among the biggest horses in the world; their ancestors were medieval warhorses, and their feet can be dinner-plate size.

Landmark moments in drinking law.Bavaria's Reinheitsgebot: The Bavarian purity law said beer could only contain water, barley and hops; yeast was added to the list after Pasteur discovered it.
Landmark moments in drinking law.Britain's Gin Act: Britain's Gin Act tried to curb the 'Gin Craze', but the heavy tax led to riots, and it was repealed after a few years.
Landmark moments in drinking law.US Whiskey Rebellion: Farmers in western Pennsylvania rebelled against a federal whiskey tax, and President Washington personally led troops to quell them.
Landmark moments in drinking law.France bans absinthe: France banned absinthe amid fears it caused madness, though the real culprit was probably its high alcohol content.
Landmark moments in drinking law.US Prohibition begins: The Volstead Act enforced the ban, and it spawned speakeasies, bootleggers and gangsters like Al Capone.
Landmark moments in drinking law.US Prohibition repealed: Prohibition ended after 13 years, and the Great Depression's need for tax revenue helped convince voters to bring back legal alcohol.
Landmark moments in drinking law.US homebrewing legalized: President Carter signed the law that made home brewing beer legal, and it allowed a craft beer industry to grow later on.
Landmark moments in drinking law.US drinking-age act: This law pushed states to raise the legal drinking age to 21 by threatening to withhold highway funds.
Landmark moments in drinking law.Iceland legalizes beer: Beer had been banned in Iceland since 1915, and the day it returned, March 1, is now celebrated as Beer Day.
Landmark moments in drinking law.Absinthe returns to the US: After nearly a century, absinthe was legal again in the US, as long as it had very low levels of the compound thujone.

Things to count in sport.Bases on a baseball diamond: The 90-foot spacing between bases has stayed the same since the 1800s, a distance that still makes close plays hard to call.
Things to count in sport.Olympic rings: The rings stand for five regions, and together with the white background the colours are meant to cover every national flag.
Things to count in sport.Pockets on a pool table: Snooker and pool share this number, but the angled jaws of the cushions mean pocket size matters more than count.
Things to count in sport.Pins in ten-pin bowling: The story goes that ten-pin arrived when nine-pin bowling was banned in some US states, and adding a tenth pin dodged the ban.
Things to count in sport.Points to win the Ryder Cup: With 28 points on offer, 14.5 wins outright, while a 14-14 tie lets the holders keep the cup.
Things to count in sport.Balls on table for 8-ball: A cue ball plus fifteen object balls make up the set, and in this game players must pot either spots or stripes.
Things to count in sport.Miles in a marathon: The odd distance was set at the 1908 London Olympics so the race could run from Windsor Castle to the royal box.
Things to count in sport.Panels on a classic Telstar: The ball is a truncated icosahedron with 12 black pentagons and 20 white hexagons, designed to be readable on black and white television.
Things to count in sport.Stitches on a baseball: Each ball has two long red stitches, sewn by hand in factories, that together total 108 stitches.
Things to count in sport.Laps of the Indy 500: At 2.5 miles a lap, this is the length of the 500-mile race, and the winner traditionally drinks milk.

Normal adult values, ranked by the numbe.Blood pH: It is slightly alkaline and tightly controlled, since a small change can be dangerous.
Normal adult values, ranked by the numbe.Breaths per minute at rest: Babies breathe far faster, around 30 to 60 times a minute.
Normal adult values, ranked by the numbe.Body temperature (°C): This figure dates from a 19th-century study, and modern averages are slightly lower, around 36.6.
Normal adult values, ranked by the numbe.Resting heart rate (bpm): Trained athletes often have lower rates, sometimes in the 40s.
Normal adult values, ranked by the numbe.Fasting blood sugar (mg/dL): Readings of 126 or more on two tests suggest diabetes.
Normal adult values, ranked by the numbe.Average IQ: It is defined as 100, and tests are re-normed, as scores have drifted upward by the Flynn effect.
Normal adult values, ranked by the numbe.Systolic blood pressure: This is the top number, the pressure when the heart squeezes, and the bottom number is measured between beats.
Normal adult values, ranked by the numbe.Blood sodium (mmol/L): Even a small change is dangerous, and sodium helps nerves fire and water balance.
Normal adult values, ranked by the numbe.Total cholesterol (mg/dL): Your liver makes most of your cholesterol, and the rest comes from food.
Normal adult values, ranked by the numbe.Platelets per microliter: These are fragments of giant cells in the bone marrow, and they make clots.

How many eyes?.Blind cave fish: Cave populations of the Mexican tetra lost their eyes over generations, while river populations of the same species can see.
How many eyes?.Human: Each eye has a blind spot where the optic nerve exits, but your brain fills the gap so smoothly you don't notice it.
How many eyes?.Tuatara: This New Zealand reptile has a third, light-sensing eye under the skin of its head, which fades with age.
How many eyes?.Honeybee: Besides two big compound eyes, bees have three tiny eyes on top of the head that help gauge light and navigate.
How many eyes?.Brown recluse spider: Most spiders have eight eyes, but this one has six, arranged in three pairs.
How many eyes?.Wolf spider: Its two large eyes reflect light, so a torch at night makes the ground sparkle where wolf spiders are.
How many eyes?.Horseshoe crab: Besides its ten eyes, this ancient animal has copper-based blue blood that is used to test vaccines for contamination.
How many eyes?.Box jellyfish: Despite having no brain, some of its eyes have lenses, retinas and corneas.
How many eyes?.Scallop: Its eyes use mirrors, not lenses, to focus light, and they ring the edge of its shell.
How many eyes?.Chiton (Acanthopleura): Their eyes have lenses made of aragonite mineral, one of the few animals to use rock-like lenses.

How high did nature reach?.Strokkur geyser jet: Strokkur in Iceland erupts every few minutes and is reliable enough that visitors rarely wait long for a show.
How high did nature reach?.Old Faithful jet: Old Faithful in Yellowstone erupts about every 90 minutes and is one of the most predictable geysers on Earth.
How high did nature reach?.Steamboat Geyser jet: Steamboat in Yellowstone is the tallest active geyser in the world, but its giant eruptions come unpredictably, sometimes years apart.
How high did nature reach?.Tallest tree (Hyperion): Hyperion, a coast redwood in California, is the tallest known living tree. Its exact location is kept secret to protect it.
How high did nature reach?.Waimangu Geyser (1900s): Waimangu in New Zealand erupted for just four years, around 1900-1904, and was probably the largest geyser ever recorded.
How high did nature reach?.Lituya Bay wave run-up: In 1958 an earthquake sent a rockslide into Alaska's Lituya Bay, and a wave surged 524 m up the hillside, the highest ever recorded.
How high did nature reach?.Thunderstorm cloud tops: Big storm clouds can climb to 15 km or more, higher than most airliners fly, which is why pilots steer around them.
How high did nature reach?.Mount St. Helens ash column: The 1980 eruption of Mount St. Helens threw an ash column about 24 km high and darkened skies hundreds of kilometers away.
How high did nature reach?.Pinatubo eruption plume: Pinatubo's 1991 eruption in the Philippines pushed material into the stratosphere and cooled the whole planet by about half a degree.
How high did nature reach?.Hunga Tonga eruption plume: The 2022 Hunga Tonga eruption sent a plume into the mesosphere, the highest ever observed, and its shock wave circled the globe.

Viking destinations, by distance from Os.Hedeby: A major Viking trading town in what is now northern Germany, near Schleswig, and an early hub for Baltic trade. It was destroyed in 1066.
Viking destinations, by distance from Os.Lindisfarne: The 793 raid on this Northumbrian monastery is traditionally taken as the start of the Viking Age.
Viking destinations, by distance from Os.Dublin: Vikings built a longphort here around 841. The name Dublin comes from 'Dyflin', from the Irish 'black pool'.
Viking destinations, by distance from Os.Kyiv: Swedish Vikings known as the Rus' travelled the rivers to Kyiv, which became the heart of Kievan Rus.
Viking destinations, by distance from Os.Constantinople: The Byzantine emperor's elite Varangian Guard recruited Norse warriors, who even carved runes into Hagia Sophia.
Viking destinations, by distance from Os.Seville: Vikings raided Seville in 844, but the Moorish rulers drove them off after heavy losses.
Viking destinations, by distance from Os.Brattahlíð, Greenland: Erik the Red's estate in Greenland. Norse settlers lived on the island for about 500 years before vanishing.
Viking destinations, by distance from Os.Jerusalem: Norway's King Sigurd I went there on crusade around 1110 and was nicknamed Jorsalfare, 'Jerusalem-farer'.
Viking destinations, by distance from Os.Baghdad: Silver coins from the Abbasid caliphate's Baghdad turn up in Viking hoards across Scandinavia.
Viking destinations, by distance from Os.L'Anse aux Meadows: The only confirmed Norse settlement in North America, on Newfoundland, dated to around the year 1000, and now a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

Particles by mass.Photon: A light particle with no mass, so it always moves at the speed of light in a vacuum.
Particles by mass.Electron: Discovered by J.J. Thomson in 1897; a proton is about 1,836 times heavier.
Particles by mass.Muon: A heavier cousin of the electron that lives only about two microseconds, yet reaches the ground from cosmic rays thanks to time dilation.
Particles by mass.Charged pion: Hideki Yukawa predicted it in 1935 as the carrier of the force binding the nucleus; it decays within nanoseconds.
Particles by mass.Proton: Made of two up quarks and one down quark, though most of its mass comes from the energy binding them together.
Particles by mass.Tau lepton: The heaviest lepton, about 3,500 times an electron, and it lasts less than a trillionth of a second.
Particles by mass.W boson: It carries the weak force behind radioactive beta decay, and was discovered at CERN in 1983.
Particles by mass.Z boson: The neutral partner of the W, found at CERN in 1983; measuring it showed there are three light types of neutrino.
Particles by mass.Higgs boson: Found at CERN's Large Hadron Collider in 2012, it confirmed the field that gives other particles their mass.
Particles by mass.Top quark: The heaviest known elementary particle, roughly as heavy as a gold atom, found at Fermilab in 1995.

Fill in the number in these famous title.The ___ Musketeers: In Dumas's novel there are really four musketeers, since d'Artagnan joins Athos, Porthos and Aramis.
Fill in the number in these famous title.Slaughterhouse-___: Kurt Vonnegut was a POW in Dresden, held in a slaughterhouse, during the firebombing.
Fill in the number in these famous title.Catch-___: Joseph Heller first titled it Catch-18, but changed it to avoid clashing with Leon Uris's Mila 18.
Fill in the number in these famous title.The ___ Steps (Buchan): John Buchan wrote this as a 'shocker', a fast-paced chase through Scotland.
Fill in the number in these famous title.___ Shades of Grey: E. L. James began the series as Twilight fan fiction.
Fill in the number in these famous title.Around the World in ___ Days: Jules Verne's Phileas Fogg wins his bet because he gains a day crossing the date line without noticing.
Fill in the number in these famous title.The Hundred and ___ Dalmatians: Dodie Smith's book starts with 15 puppies, and it all adds up to 101 in the end.
Fill in the number in these famous title.Fahrenheit ___: Ray Bradbury wrote that it is the temperature at which book paper burns.
Fill in the number in these famous title.Orwell's ___: Orwell is said to have chosen the year by reversing 1948, when he finished it.
Fill in the number in these famous title.___ Leagues Under the Sea: The 20,000 leagues is the distance traveled, not depth; the ocean's deepest point is only around three leagues down.

When these soft drinks were first poured.Dr Pepper: Invented by Waco, Texas pharmacist Charles Alderton, it predates Coca-Cola and remains America's oldest major soft drink.
When these soft drinks were first poured.Coca-Cola: Atlanta pharmacist John Pemberton created it; in the first year, sales averaged only about nine drinks a day.
When these soft drinks were first poured.Pepsi: Caleb Bradham invented it in New Bern, North Carolina, selling it first as 'Brad's Drink' before renaming it in 1898.
When these soft drinks were first poured.Irn-Bru: The Scottish soda, originally 'Iron Brew', often outsells Coca-Cola in Scotland, a rare feat.
When these soft drinks were first poured.7 Up: It launched just before the 1929 crash as a lemon-lime soda with lithium citrate, a mood-stabilising drug, in the recipe.
When these soft drinks were first poured.Fanta: It was created in Nazi Germany in 1940, when the wartime embargo cut off Coca-Cola syrup; its name comes from 'Fantasie'.
When these soft drinks were first poured.Sprite: Coca-Cola launched this lemon-lime soda in 1961 to compete directly with 7 Up.
When these soft drinks were first poured.Gatorade: University of Florida researchers developed it to refill athletes' lost fluids, and named it after the Florida Gators.
When these soft drinks were first poured.Diet Coke: It was the first new Coca-Cola brand to carry the company's name in almost a century, and it soon became the top diet soda in America.
When these soft drinks were first poured.Coca-Cola Zero: The no-sugar cola was marketed at men who rejected 'diet' drinks, and was renamed Coca-Cola Zero Sugar in 2017.

Cold War flashpoints, in order.Berlin Airlift: Candy bomber Gail Halvorsen dropped chocolate on tiny parachutes to Berlin's children during it.
Cold War flashpoints, in order.Hungarian Uprising: Soviet tanks crushed it, and about 200,000 people fled the country.
Cold War flashpoints, in order.Sputnik launched: The first artificial satellite beeped overhead and launched the space race.
Cold War flashpoints, in order.U-2 spy plane shot down: Pilot Gary Powers was shot down over Sverdlovsk in May and later swapped for a Soviet spy.
Cold War flashpoints, in order.Bay of Pigs: CIA-trained exiles invaded Cuba and were defeated within three days.
Cold War flashpoints, in order.Cuban Missile Crisis: Submarine officer Vasili Arkhipov reportedly refused to authorize a nuclear torpedo launch during it.
Cold War flashpoints, in order.Prague Spring: Alexander Dubček promised 'socialism with a human face', until Warsaw Pact tanks arrived in August.
Cold War flashpoints, in order.Soviets invade Afghanistan: The nine-year war helped lead to the US boycott of the 1980 Moscow Olympics.
Cold War flashpoints, in order.Reagan's 'Evil Empire' speech: Reagan delivered it to evangelicals in Orlando, Florida.
Cold War flashpoints, in order.Reykjavik Summit: Reagan and Gorbachev nearly agreed to abolish nuclear weapons, but talks stalled over missile defense.

Ancient sun-watching sites, by age.Goseck Circle: This German ring of wooden posts and ditches is often called the oldest known solar observatory, aligned to the winter solstice sunrise and sunset.
Ancient sun-watching sites, by age.Mnajdra temples: These Maltese temples are aligned so sunrise lights up the main doorway on the equinoxes and passes along the corners on solstices.
Ancient sun-watching sites, by age.Newgrange: In Ireland, sunlight enters a narrow roof-box for a few minutes around the winter solstice, lighting the tomb's chamber, older than the pyramids.
Ancient sun-watching sites, by age.Callanish stones: These standing stones on Scotland's Isle of Lewis form a cross-shaped pattern, and some think they track the Moon's long cycle.
Ancient sun-watching sites, by age.Stonehenge sarsens: At the solstices, the sun aligns with the monument's main axis, and the large stones weigh up to about 25 tonnes.
Ancient sun-watching sites, by age.Chankillo towers: In Peru's desert, thirteen towers stand in a row along a ridge, forming a solar calendar by marking where the sun rises each day.
Ancient sun-watching sites, by age.Pyramid of the Sun: Teotihuacan's largest pyramid is among the biggest in the Americas, and the city it towers over was among the largest in the ancient world.
Ancient sun-watching sites, by age.Chichén Itzá's El Castillo: At the equinoxes, shadows on its stairway form a serpent that seems to slither down, linked to the god Kukulkan.
Ancient sun-watching sites, by age.Angkor Wat: Cambodia's vast temple faces west, unusually, and at the spring equinox the sun rises directly over its central tower.
Ancient sun-watching sites, by age.Machu Picchu: Built for Inca ruler Pachacuti, it features the Intihuatana stone, which may have been used to track the sun's position through the year.
